questions.evidence: Meera moved her hand across it, and the circle appeared on her hand instead.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Working out what made a changing patch of light.
Finding the best place to hang a classroom painting.
Learning to draw a circle without a round object.
questions.evidence: Their teacher carefully turned the mirror, and the bright circle moved across the wall.

items.title: The Dragon Who Packed Too Much
items.passage: Ravi was writing a comic about a dragon going on a picnic. Yan drew a bag full of cups, plates, books, and a huge blanket. In the next picture, the dragon tried to fly, but the bag stayed on the ground. Ravi wanted the dragon to reach a hill for its picnic. Yan suggested drawing a smaller bag, but Ravi liked all the things inside the big one. They looked at the first picture again. It showed the dragon waiting beside a little cart. Yan drew the dragon putting the bag in the cart and pulling it along the path. At the hill, the dragon opened the blanket for its friends. Ravi added one last picture of the empty cart. A sleepy rabbit had chosen it for a bed.

questions.stem: What did the dragon put in the cart?
options: The friends going to the picnic.
The books borrowed from a library.
questions.evidence: Yan drew the dragon putting the bag in the cart and pulling it along the path.

questions.stem: Why did the cart solve the problem?
options: It let the dragon move the bag without flying.
It made the picnic things fit in a smaller bag.
It showed the dragon a shorter path to the hill.
questions.evidence: Yan drew the dragon putting the bag in the cart and pulling it along the path.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Using something already in a comic to solve its story problem.
Removing extra characters to make a comic easier to follow.
Changing the place of a picnic so a comic can end sooner.
questions.evidence: It showed the dragon waiting beside a little cart.

items.title: The Unopened Box
items.passage: Mia brought a box of drawing things when she visited Tom. She had planned to teach him how to draw a horse. Tom met her at the door holding a page covered in tiny buildings. He began showing her the shops, park, and school in his paper town. Mia kept her box closed while he talked. When he pointed to an empty field, she asked what belonged there. Tom said he had not decided yet. Mia opened her box and drew a horse on a fresh piece of paper. Tom placed it in the field and drew a path leading to the town. They spent the afternoon adding animals and places for them to live. On her way home, Mia saw she had never given her drawing lesson. Her horse had found somewhere to live instead.

questions.stem: Which part of the town was empty?
questions.evidence: When he pointed to an empty field, she asked what belonged there.

questions.stem: Why did Mia wait before opening her box?
options: She had forgotten where she put her pencils.
She was listening to Tom's idea first.
She wanted Tom to guess her best-loved animal.
questions.evidence: Mia kept her box closed while he talked.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Combining two different ideas during a visit.
Finishing a drawing lesson before going outside.
Choosing which friend has made the better picture.
questions.evidence: They spent the afternoon adding animals and places for them to live.

items.title: The Photograph Corner
items.passage: Lily found a photograph of a garden in an old family album. She could see a low wall and a tree beside a little wooden seat. Ben said it looked nothing like the garden outside their window. They took the album to the window and compared the two views. The tree outside was much taller, and there was no wooden seat. Lily noticed a pale square on the wall in the photograph. The same square was still showing outside, partly hidden by leaves. Ben moved to the other end of the window and held the photograph up. From there, the wall and the tree lined up with the picture. They asked their aunt about the missing seat. She said it had broken years ago, before either child could remember it. Ben looked at the photograph again, now sure that it showed their garden.

questions.stem: What had disappeared from the garden?
questions.evidence: She said it had broken years ago, before either child could remember it.

questions.stem: What helped them work out which garden the photograph showed?
options: All the plants were exactly the same size.
A mark on the wall had stayed the same.
Someone had written the address on the picture.
questions.evidence: The same square was still showing outside, partly hidden by leaves.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Finding a familiar place in an older picture.
Planning to rebuild a garden from an old picture.
Learning how to take a photograph through glass.
questions.evidence: Ben looked at the photograph again, now sure that it showed their garden.

items.title: The Pocket Museum
items.passage: Sam was helping Zoe sort clothes before putting them away. In one coat pocket, he found a small stone and a paper ticket. Zoe remembered collecting the stone on a walk with their grandfather. The ticket was from a train journey they had taken the same day. Sam put both things on the table and asked what was in the next pocket. They found a button, a little drawing, and a folded shopping list. Zoe could remember a story for almost every object. Sam arranged them in a row and made paper labels for them. He called their table a museum of ordinary days. Zoe put the shopping list back because they still needed it. Then she added a label to the empty place where it had been. It said that this part of the museum had gone shopping.

questions.stem: Where had Zoe collected the stone?
options: On a beach with her cousin.
On a walk with her grandfather.
questions.evidence: Zoe remembered collecting the stone on a walk with their grandfather.

questions.stem: Why did Sam call the table a museum?
options: The objects were all very expensive.
The objects had stories worth showing.
The objects had all been found under the ground.
questions.evidence: Zoe could remember a story for almost every object.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Deciding which old clothes should be given away.
Making a list of things to buy on a journey.
Finding memories in things kept in pockets.
questions.evidence: He called their table a museum of ordinary days.

items.title: The Question Box
items.passage: Raj helped Ella make a box for questions about their class animal project. They put it by the door with some small pieces of paper. By lunch, there were six questions inside, all asking where the answers would appear. Raj looked at their sign and saw that it only said QUESTIONS. He added words saying the class would discuss them on Friday. Ella placed an example beside the box: How do penguins keep warm? The next morning, they opened the box and found questions about birds, cats, and frogs. One child wanted to know whether fish ever slept. Raj read every question aloud while Ella wrote them on a large page. They left room beneath each one for the class to add answers. Ella kept the six original questions too. She said those had helped them improve the box before the animal project even started.

questions.stem: When would the class discuss the questions?
questions.evidence: He added words saying the class would discuss them on Friday.

questions.stem: Why did the first questions ask where answers would appear?
options: The class had already answered every animal question.
The children had lost the page of written answers.
The original sign had not explained the next step.
questions.evidence: Raj looked at their sign and saw that it only said QUESTIONS.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Choosing the easiest animal questions for a class test.
Finding a larger box when too many questions arrive.
Making an invitation clearer so people can take part.
questions.evidence: He added words saying the class would discuss them on Friday.

items.title: The Best Cat Picture
items.passage: Nina wanted a photograph of her cat sitting beside a plant pot. Omar held the camera while she placed a toy near the pot. The cat walked over, looked at the toy, and sat facing the other way. Nina moved around the pot, hoping to catch its face. The cat turned again, following a bird outside the window. Omar lowered the camera and watched for a moment. Then he moved beside Nina and took a picture from behind the cat. The photograph showed two pointed ears, the window, and a tiny bird beyond the glass. Nina began to say that the face was missing. But she stopped when she noticed how clearly the picture showed what the cat was watching. She asked Omar to send her that one. Under it, she wrote that their cat had chosen the view.

questions.stem: What was the cat watching outside?
questions.evidence: The cat turned again, following a bird outside the window.

questions.stem: Why did Nina change her mind about the photograph?
options: It showed something interesting about the cat's attention.
It showed the cat's face more clearly than she expected.
It showed that the plant pot was in the wrong place.
questions.evidence: But she stopped when she noticed how clearly the picture showed what the cat was watching.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Teaching a cat to follow instructions for a photograph.
Learning to take pictures without looking through a camera.
Discovering that an unexpected picture can be worth keeping.
questions.evidence: She asked Omar to send her that one.

items.title: The Ant Route
items.passage: Amir and Sara watched ants crossing a dry patch of ground in the school garden. They stayed beside their teacher and kept their hands away from the insects. Sara drew a line on paper to show where the ants were going. At first, she made the line straight. Amir pointed to a fallen leaf that several ants were walking around. Sara changed her line to bend around a leaf shape. Then they noticed a second group taking a different route past a small rock. Instead of rubbing out the first line, Sara added another. By the end of their visit, the page looked like a little road map. Back in class, Amir tried following one line with his finger. He stopped at a crossing and asked which way to go. Sara laughed and said their map needed another visit before they could answer that.

questions.stem: What did several ants walk around?
questions.evidence: Amir pointed to a fallen leaf that several ants were walking around.

questions.stem: Why did Sara keep the first line?
options: She could not remember where the first route went.
She had seen more than one route being used.
She wanted the map to look like a star.
questions.evidence: Then they noticed a second group taking a different route past a small rock.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Guiding insects along a route chosen by children.
Making a map that shows every path in a garden.
Changing a drawing to match what is being observed.
questions.evidence: Instead of rubbing out the first line, Sara added another.

items.title: The Hidden Rule
items.passage: Max arranged four picture cards in a row and asked Priya to add another. The cards showed a banana, a lemon, a yellow hat, and a yellow bus. Priya chose a yellow bird from the pile and placed it at the end. Max nodded and asked how she had worked out his rule. Priya said all the pictures were yellow. Max explained that his rule had been things he had seen that morning. He had seen a yellow bird too, so her choice happened to fit. They looked at the cards and saw that both explanations worked. Max added a picture of a blue bicycle from his morning walk. Priya smiled and changed her explanation. For the next round, she chose her own cards and kept her rule secret. This time, Max asked for one more example before giving his answer.

questions.stem: Which card did Max add after the bird?
questions.evidence: Max added a picture of a blue bicycle from his morning walk.

questions.stem: Why did Max ask for another example in the next round?
options: He had forgotten the names of the pictured objects.
He wanted Priya to put the cards in order by their first letters.
He knew one set of cards could fit different rules.
questions.evidence: They looked at the cards and saw that both explanations worked.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Remembering every object seen during a morning walk.
Finding that more than one explanation can fit the same clues.
Learning a new way to name objects in a card game.
questions.evidence: They looked at the cards and saw that both explanations worked.

items.title: The Recorded Rain
items.passage: Jack and Aisha wanted rain sounds for a story they were recording. They listened at the window, but the real rain was too quiet for their tablet. Jack shook a box of dry rice, and Aisha listened with her eyes closed. She said it sounded more like a short shower than a whole rainy afternoon. Jack shook it for longer, but his arm soon became tired. Aisha brought a second box and filled it with a little rice. They took turns, starting one box before the other stopped. On the recording, the rain went on without a sudden gap. Jack read the story while Aisha played their sound back. At the end, the rain slowly faded as they had planned. Outside, the real rain had stopped as well. They opened the window and listened to the quiet ending that nobody had recorded.

questions.stem: What did Jack shake to make rain sounds?
questions.evidence: Jack shook a box of dry rice, and Aisha listened with her eyes closed.

questions.stem: Why did using two boxes help?
options: One could make the story words easier to hear.
One could keep the real rain away from the tablet.
One could continue while the other person rested.
questions.evidence: They took turns, starting one box before the other stopped.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Comparing different weather reports before recording them.
Working together to make a sound for a story.
Learning why real rain is sometimes quiet and sometimes loud.
questions.evidence: On the recording, the rain went on without a sudden gap.

items.title: The Finished Corner
items.passage: Meera and Dan were helping their class make a huge picture of a park. Meera carefully drew flowers in one corner while Dan painted a path. When their teacher asked whether they were finished, Meera shook her head. She could still see places where more flowers might fit. Dan had already put his brush down, but he waited beside her. He asked where someone in the picture would walk to reach the flowers. Meera looked at the path and noticed it stopped before her corner. She put down her flower pencil and helped him extend the path. Now it curved around the flowers and joined the rest of the park. Meera stepped back far enough to see the whole picture. She decided that her corner did not need another flower. It had needed a way for the rest of the picture to reach it.

questions.stem: What was Dan painting?
questions.evidence: Meera carefully drew flowers in one corner while Dan painted a path.

questions.stem: Why did Meera stop adding flowers?
options: She saw how her corner connected with the whole picture.
She had used all the flower paint in the classroom.
She wanted Dan to finish the flowers without her.
questions.evidence: Meera stepped back far enough to see the whole picture.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Looking at a whole project to decide what it still needs.
Learning to draw flowers by copying a classmate's work.
Finishing a picture quickly before the teacher takes it away.
questions.evidence: She decided that her corner did not need another flower.

items.title: The Letter to a Robot
items.reviewNote: 'What was in the last box?' önceki şeyler kutu değil -> 'What did the robot bring in the end?'
items.passage: Ravi wrote a letter to the robot in his new story. He asked it to bring him something that would make a rainy day better. Yan drew the robot arriving with a large umbrella. Ravi said that was useful, but his character had planned to stay indoors. Yan drew the robot bringing a board game instead. Now Ravi pointed out that the character was alone until the afternoon. They looked back at the letter and saw how little it told the robot. Ravi added that the character liked drawing and had no blue pencil. Yan drew a small box holding a blue pencil and some clean paper. In the last picture, the character drew a sky full of blue clouds. The robot waited beside him, holding the umbrella over the drawing. Ravi kept that part because it made him laugh.

questions.stem: What was in the last box?
questions.evidence: Yan drew a small box holding a blue pencil and some clean paper.

questions.stem: Why did Ravi add details to the letter?
options: The robot needed to know more about what would help.
The robot could only read very long messages.
The robot had lost the character's address.
questions.evidence: They looked back at the letter and saw how little it told the robot.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Teaching a robot to draw clouds in different shapes.
Making a request clearer by adding useful details.
Choosing a game that can be played in rainy weather.
questions.evidence: Ravi added that the character liked drawing and had no blue pencil.

items.title: The Page Nobody Chose
items.passage: Kofi and Rita were choosing pictures from a book to copy for a display. Kofi chose a bright bird, and Rita chose a house covered in flowers. They passed a plain picture of a wooden bench without stopping. Later, Kofi looked for somewhere to put his bird in their shared drawing. Rita suggested a tree, but the page already had two large trees. They turned back through the book and came to the bench again. Kofi drew it between the trees and placed the bird on its back. Rita added a person sitting there, looking towards the house covered in flowers. The plain bench now joined the different parts of their picture. When the teacher asked which book picture had helped most, they looked at each other. Then both pointed to the page they had nearly skipped. Rita placed a bookmark there before returning the book.

questions.stem: What did Rita choose to copy first?
questions.evidence: Kofi chose a bright bird, and Rita chose a house covered in flowers.

questions.stem: Why did they point to the bench page?
options: It had helped their separate drawings work together.
It had been the easiest page to find in the book.
It had shown them how to draw every kind of bird.
questions.evidence: The plain bench now joined the different parts of their picture.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Discovering the value of something that first seemed uninteresting.
Choosing the brightest picture for a classroom competition.
Learning to copy every page of a library book.
questions.evidence: Then both pointed to the page they had nearly skipped.

items.title: The Door That Stayed Open
items.passage: Tom and Mia built a little shop from a large cardboard box. They made a door from a separate piece of card and attached it with tape. Mia put toy fruit on the shelves while Tom wrote prices on paper. When they opened the door, it knocked the nearest shelf and sent apples onto the floor. Tom picked up the apples and tried opening the door less widely. Now the toy bear carrying a shopping bag could not fit through. Mia moved the shelf away from the door, leaving a clear space behind it. They tested the door again before putting the apples back. This time, it opened fully and the shelf stayed still. Tom sent the bear inside with its bag. Mia asked what it wanted to buy. Tom said the bear would start with the apples, since it already knew where they were.

questions.stem: What fell when the door hit the shelf?
questions.evidence: When they opened the door, it knocked the nearest shelf and sent apples onto the floor.

questions.stem: Why was opening the door only a little not a good solution?
options: It left too little room for a shopper to enter.
It made the shelf too high for Mia to reach.
It stopped Tom from writing the prices clearly.
questions.evidence: Now the toy bear carrying a shopping bag could not fit through.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Choosing which fruit a pretend shop should sell first.
Making a shop smaller so it fits on a classroom table.
Testing and changing a model so its parts work together.
questions.evidence: This time, it opened fully and the shelf stayed still.

items.title: The Recipe Picture
items.passage: Lily wanted to show Ben how she made her usual fruit bowl. She drew a banana, some grapes, and a spoon on a page. Ben looked at the drawing and put a whole banana beside the grapes in a bowl. Lily smiled and showed him the small banana pieces she had meant. He asked how he could have known that from her picture. Lily drew three little pictures below: peeling the banana, breaking it into pieces, and adding grapes. Ben followed them and stirred the fruit with the spoon. He drew one more picture at the end, showing two bowls. They divided the fruit between them and sat down at the table. Lily put the picture recipe beside her bowl. Ben added two smiling faces below the last step. Now the page showed not only what went in, but what happened afterwards too.

questions.stem: What did Ben add to the picture recipe?
options: A picture of a tall glass.
questions.evidence: He drew one more picture at the end, showing two bowls.

questions.stem: Why did Lily add the smaller pictures?
options: Ben wanted to change the grapes for another fruit.
The first picture had not shown what to do with the fruit.
The banana was too small to see in the first drawing.
questions.evidence: Lily drew three little pictures below: peeling the banana, breaking it into pieces, and adding grapes.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Choosing different fruit because a first recipe tasted unpleasant.
Turning a picture of ingredients into instructions someone can follow.
Learning to draw food so it looks exactly like a real meal.
questions.evidence: Ben followed them and stirred the fruit with the spoon.

items.title: The Audience of One
items.passage: Sam had prepared a funny show for three friends after school. Only Zoe could come because the others had music lessons. He looked at the three empty chairs and began putting his paper hat away. Zoe asked if a show needed three people watching before it could start. Sam thought about that, then put the hat back on. He started the first part of his show while Zoe sat in the middle chair. She laughed at a moment when he had expected everyone to be quiet. Sam stopped, then tried moving again more slowly. Zoe laughed even harder and asked how he had done it. After the show, they worked on that part together. Sam wrote down the new part so he could remember it next time. The other two chairs had stayed empty, but he had found something worth keeping for a bigger audience.

questions.stem: Why could the other friends not come?
questions.evidence: Only Zoe could come because the others had music lessons.

questions.stem: Why did Sam write down the new part?
options: Zoe had forgotten all the words of the first show.
Zoe's laughter helped him find a part that worked well.
The teacher had asked him to copy a whole play.
questions.evidence: Zoe laughed even harder and asked how he had done it.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Finding value in performing for a smaller audience than expected.
Choosing the funniest costume before inviting friends to a show.
Learning why music lessons are more popular than acting.
questions.evidence: Sam wrote down the new part so he could remember it next time.

items.title: The Partner Who Waited
items.passage: Raj and Ella were making a poster about animals that live in cold places. Raj quickly wrote a title and began drawing a penguin. Ella sat with her pencil above the paper but did not start. Raj asked if she wanted him to draw her part too. She shook her head and pointed to a photograph in their book. She was studying how the penguin held its feet while walking. Raj looked at his own drawing and noticed that both feet pointed the same way. He waited while Ella drew one foot lifted above the ground. Her penguin looked as though it was taking a careful step. Raj added another bird behind it and changed his title to a question about walking. They spent the rest of the lesson watching short clips chosen by their teacher. The poster had started slowly, but it now had a question they both wanted to answer.

questions.stem: What was Ella studying in the photograph?
questions.evidence: She was studying how the penguin held its feet while walking.

questions.stem: Why had Ella not started drawing straight away?
options: She was looking carefully before deciding how to draw.
She wanted Raj to finish the whole poster for her.
She had forgotten which animal their poster was about.
questions.evidence: She shook her head and pointed to a photograph in their book.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Finishing an animal poster faster by dividing the drawing equally.
Choosing an easier animal when a first drawing goes wrong.
Noticing that taking time to look can lead to a useful question.
questions.evidence: The poster had started slowly, but it now had a question they both wanted to answer.

items.title: The Sound at the Door
items.passage: Nina heard a soft scratching sound beside the kitchen door. She thought their dog wanted to come inside from the hall. Omar opened the door, but the dog was asleep on a mat farther away. He closed it again, and the scratching returned. Nina stood still and watched the bottom of the door. A loose paper notice hung there, brushing the floor when air moved through the gap. Omar held the paper against the door, and the sound stopped. They moved the notice higher and fixed it with another piece of tape. When they opened and closed the door, nothing scratched. The dog woke up and came over to see them. Nina laughed and said they had answered the paper before the dog. Omar opened the door once more and let the real visitor walk into the kitchen.

questions.stem: Where was the dog when Omar first opened the door?
questions.evidence: Omar opened the door, but the dog was asleep on a mat farther away.

questions.stem: What showed that the paper caused the sound?
options: Holding it still stopped the scratching.
The dog woke up when they spoke.
The notice had writing on both sides.
questions.evidence: Omar held the paper against the door, and the sound stopped.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Teaching a dog to wait quietly outside a kitchen.
Checking a first guess to find the real source of a sound.
Writing a clearer notice so visitors can find the right door.
questions.evidence: They moved the notice higher and fixed it with another piece of tape.

items.title: The Flower After Lunch
items.passage: Amir drew a flower in the school garden before the morning lesson. Sara planned to draw the same flower after lunch. When she arrived, she found that it looked different from Amir's picture. Some petals had opened farther, and a shadow now fell across the ground beside it. Sara wondered if Amir had drawn a different plant. He showed her a bent leaf that appeared in his picture and on the plant. Sara drew her picture, then asked their teacher if they could draw it again later. Before going home, they made one drawing together and wrote the time below it. They added times to the earlier pictures and placed all three in order on the wall. The bent leaf showed that the changing flower was still the same plant. Amir added a space for another drawing. They wanted to see what the same flower would look like on a cloudy morning.

questions.stem: What helped them find the same plant?
questions.evidence: He showed her a bent leaf that appeared in his picture and on the plant.

questions.stem: Why did they write the time below the drawings?
options: To connect each view with when they saw it.
To show how quickly each child could finish drawing.
To remember when their teacher wanted the pictures back.
questions.evidence: Before going home, they made one drawing together and wrote the time below it.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Finding which child makes the best flower drawings.
Moving a plant to different places to make it grow faster.
Following changes in one flower by drawing it at different times.
questions.evidence: They added times to the earlier pictures and placed all three in order on the wall.

items.title: The Score on the Back
items.passage: Max and Priya played a guessing game with cards they had made themselves. Priya won the first round and wrote her score on the back of a card. In the next round, Max noticed that card whenever it was face down. He remembered the animal on its other side and guessed it at once. Priya started to clap, then saw where he was looking. Max explained that the writing had given the answer away. They checked all the cards and found a small blue mark on another one. Priya placed each card inside the same kind of paper cover, with the picture hidden until opened. They wrote future scores in a separate book. When they played again, Max had to listen to the clues before guessing. He missed the first animal but laughed at his mistake. This round felt more like the game they had meant to make.

questions.stem: Where did Priya write her first score?
options: On the lid of the box.
On a page in her book.
On the back of a card.
questions.evidence: Priya won the first round and wrote her score on the back of a card.

questions.stem: Why did the paper covers help?
options: They made the animal pictures larger to look at.
They hid marks that showed which card was which.
They reminded each player how many points they had.
questions.evidence: Priya placed each card inside the same kind of paper cover, with the picture hidden until opened.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Making animal clues easier after both players forget the answers.
Finding a quicker way to add scores at the end of a game.
Removing a secret clue so a guessing game works properly.
questions.evidence: When they played again, Max had to listen to the clues before guessing.

items.title: The Song from Next Door
items.passage: Jack was trying to remember a tune he had heard at school. He hummed the first few notes, then stopped at the same place each time. Aisha listened from the next room while she sorted her books. After several tries, she hummed a possible ending back to him. Jack said it was not the ending he remembered, but asked her to sing it again. He joined her, changing one note where their voices did not fit together. They repeated the new tune until neither had to stop. Later, Jack found the original song in a recording from their teacher. Its ending was quite different from the one they had made. Aisha asked if they should change theirs to match. Jack listened to both and shook his head. They gave their version a new name and kept the school song for another day.

questions.stem: Where was Aisha when she first heard Jack?
questions.evidence: Aisha listened from the next room while she sorted her books.

questions.stem: Why did they give their version a new name?
options: They could not find the original recording anywhere.
Their teacher had told them to stop singing the old song.
It had become a different tune they wanted to keep.
questions.evidence: Its ending was quite different from the one they had made.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Learning an old song exactly as the teacher recorded it.
Finding a quiet room where two people can sing without stopping.
Turning an incomplete memory into something new together.
questions.evidence: They gave their version a new name and kept the school song for another day.

items.title: The Longer Shadow
items.passage: Meera and Dan stood in the school playground with their teacher early one morning. Dan pointed to his shadow and said it was much taller than he was. Meera marked its end with chalk while he stood beside a painted square. After lunch, they returned to the same square and stood in the same places. Dan's shadow no longer reached the chalk mark. He wondered whether Meera had moved the mark while he was in class. She pointed to her own shadow, which was shorter too. Their teacher asked them to compare where the sunlight came from without looking at the sun. They noticed that the light now fell from higher in the sky. Meera added a second chalk mark and wrote afternoon beside it. Dan looked between the marks and smiled. He had stayed the same height, but his shadow had told a different story.

questions.stem: What did Meera use to mark the shadow's end?
questions.evidence: Meera marked its end with chalk while he stood beside a painted square.

questions.stem: Why was moving the first mark not a good explanation?
options: Dan had grown taller during the lesson.
Both children's shadows had become shorter.
The painted square had changed its shape.
questions.evidence: She pointed to her own shadow, which was shorter too.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: Finding the tallest child by measuring shadows at different times.
Choosing a sunny place to draw pictures on the playground.
Comparing observations to understand a change during the day.
questions.evidence: Meera added a second chalk mark and wrote afternoon beside it.

items.title: The Wrong Sound
items.passage: Amir was making a short film with his toy animals. Lily helped him record the sounds on a tablet. They needed footsteps for a tiny mouse crossing a kitchen floor. Amir tapped two pencils on the table, but the sound was much too loud. On the screen, the little mouse seemed as heavy as an elephant. Lily laughed and asked him to play that part again. Amir reached for the button that would remove the sound. Then he stopped and looked at the toy elephant beside the tablet. items.title: The Second Map
items.passage: Ravi drew a map of the classroom for a treasure game. Nina had to follow it to find a paper star. He marked a table, a bookcase, and a chair, then drew a line between them. Nina followed the line and stopped at the wrong chair. There were four chairs that looked exactly like the one on his map. Ravi pointed towards the right chair, but Nina asked him to wait. She wanted to try without being shown the answer. Ravi looked around and noticed a picture of a whale above the right chair. He added the whale to his map and gave it back. This time, Nina found the star under the seat. She turned it over and drew a tiny whale on the back. Ravi put it beside his map, ready for the next player.

items.title: A Place in the Picture
items.passage: Kofi and Ella were making a picture for the school library. Kofi painted a huge tree, while Ella drew children reading beneath it. When they put the two parts together, one branch covered a child's book. Kofi offered to paint over the branch, but he liked its crooked shape. Ella moved her drawing lower, and now the child's feet disappeared below the paper. For a while, neither of them changed anything. Then Ella took a clean sheet and drew the child sitting higher, with legs hanging down. She placed the new drawing on the branch. The child was reading in the tree, with the book clearly in view. Kofi added a bird looking at the open pages. They left the rest of the children on the ground. Their picture now had one reader with a very unusual seat.

items.title: The Empty Square
items.passage: Yan and Rita made a board game on a large sheet of paper. Every square told players to do something, such as clap twice or name an animal. One square near the end was empty. Yan reached for a pen, but Rita suggested testing the game first. When Yan landed on the empty square, he waited for an instruction. Rita said he could make one up just for that turn. He asked everyone to speak like a robot until his next turn. Rita laughed so much that her robot voice came out in little squeaks. They played again, and this time Rita landed there. She asked Yan to name an animal beginning with the first letter of his name. He thought for a moment, then said yak. After the game, Yan wrote just two words in the empty square: YOUR IDEA.
